﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾

*Bism Allah*: The *ba'* (ب, "in") is a particle that governs the noun after it in the genitive, like *min* ("from") and *'an* ("about"). The word it is attached to is omitted, because the context indicates it. Its estimated form is: "I begin in the name of God," or "Say: In the name of God." The *alif* is dropped from *ism* for the sake of lightness and because the word is used so frequently. The *ba'* is elongated. Al-Qutaybi said: so that the opening of the words of the Book of God begins with a letter that is glorified. 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, may God have mercy on him, used to say to his scribes: "Elongate the *ba'*, show the *sin* [and] separate them, and round the *mim*, in glorification of the Book of God, may He be exalted." It was also said: when they dropped the *alif*, they gave the length of the *alif* to the *ba'*, so that it would signal the dropping of the *alif*. Do you not see that when the *alif* was written in *Iqra' bi-smi rabbika* (96:1), the *ba'* was returned to its normal form? The *alif* is not dropped when the word *ism* is joined to other than God, nor when it is used with other than the *ba'*.

*Ism* is the named (*musamma*), its essence and its very self. God the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, We give you good tidings of a boy whose name is Yahya﴾ (19:7). He informed that his name is Yahya, then he addressed the name, saying: "O Yahya." And He said: ﴿You worship not besides Him except names you have named﴾ (12:40), and He meant the objects of worship, because they used to worship the named things. And He said: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ (87:1), and "Blessed is the name of your Lord" [[From manuscript (B).]]. Then *ism* is also used of the naming itself, so its use for the naming is more common than its use for the named [[Omitted from manuscript (A).]]. If it is asked: what is the meaning of God naming Himself? It is said: it is a teaching for the servants on how they should begin the recitation.

They differed concerning its derivation. Al-Mubarrad, from the Basran grammarians, said: it is derived from *sumuw*, which means elevation, as if it rises above its meaning and dominates it, its meaning being beneath it. Tha'lab, from the Kufan grammarians, said: it is derived from *wasm* and *simah*, which is a mark, as if it were a mark of its meaning. The first view is sounder, because its diminutive is *sumayy*, whereas if it were from *simah* its diminutive would be *wusayim*, as is said of *wa'd* (promise), whose diminutive is *wu'ayd*. Its conjugation is *sammaytu* ("I named"), and if it were from *wasm* it would be said *wasamtu*.

God's words: ﴿Allah﴾. Al-Khalil and a group said: it is a proper name specific to God, Mighty and Majestic, with no derivation, like the proper names of servants such as Zayd and 'Amr. Another group said: it is derived. They then differed about its derivation. It was said: from *alaha*, *ilahah*, meaning he worshipped with worship. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, read ﴿and your worship﴾ (7:127) as *wa-alihatak*, meaning your worship. The meaning is that He alone deserves to be worshipped to the exclusion of others. It was also said that its origin is *Ilah*, as God, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And there was not with Him any other god; otherwise, each god would have taken away what he created﴾ (23:91). Al-Mubarrad said: it is from the saying of the Arabs *alihtu ila fulan*, meaning I found tranquillity in him. The poet said: "I found tranquillity in her while events were many." So it is as if creatures find rest in Him and are reassured by His remembrance. It is also said *alihtu ilayhi*, meaning I sought refuge in him. The poet said: "I sought refuge in her while the riding-camels stood still." It was also said that the origin of *ilah* is *wilah*, and the *waw* was replaced by a *hamzah*, as in *wishah* and *ishah*. Its derivation is from *walah* (bewilderment), because servants are bewildered toward Him, that is, they cry out to Him in hardships and seek Him in their needs, as every child is bewildered toward its mother. It was also said that it is from *walah*, which is the loss of reason due to the absence of one who is dear to you.

His words: ﴿the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: they are two tender names, one of them more tender than the other. They differed concerning them. Some said: they have one meaning, like *nadman* and *nadim* (both meaning "companion"), and their meaning is "the one possessed of mercy." Mentioning one after the other is to encourage (*tat'im*) [[In the original: *ta'zim*, "glorification."]] the hearts of those who desire. Al-Mubarrad said: it is one favour after another and one bounty after another. Others distinguished between them, saying: *al-Rahman* has the sense of generality and *al-Rahim* the sense of particularity. Thus *al-Rahman* means the provider in this world, and this is general for all creation. *Al-Rahim* means the pardoner in the Hereafter, and forgiveness in the Hereafter is specific to the believers. For this reason it is said in supplication: "O Most Gracious of this world and Most Merciful of the Hereafter." So *al-Rahman* is the one whose mercy reaches creatures in general, and *al-Rahim* is the one whose mercy reaches them in particular. For this reason, others than God may be called *rahim* but no one other than God is called *rahman*. So *al-Rahman* is general in meaning and specific in wording, while *al-Rahim* is general in wording and specific in meaning. Mercy (*rahmah*) is God's willing good for its recipients. It was also said that it is abstaining from punishing one who deserves it and conferring good upon one who does not deserve it. Thus on the first view it is an attribute of essence (*sifat dhat*), and on the second it is an attribute of action (*sifat fi'l*) [[In the original: *al-fi'l*.]].

They differed concerning whether the basmalah is a verse. The reciters of Medina and Basra and the jurists of Kufa held that it is not part of the Fatihah nor of any other surah, and that beginning with it is for blessing and auspiciousness. The reciters of Mecca and Kufa and most of the jurists of the Hijaz held that it is part of the Fatihah but not part of the other surahs, and that it was written as a separator. A group held that it is part of the Fatihah and of every surah except Surat al-Tawbah. This is the view of al-Thawri, Ibn al-Mubarak and al-Shafi'i, because it is written in the codex in the script of the rest of the Qur'an.

They agreed that the Fatihah consists of seven verses. According to those who count the basmalah as part of the Fatihah, the first verse is ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, and the beginning of the last verse is ﴿the path of those﴾. Those who do not count it as part of the Fatihah say that its beginning is "All praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds," and the beginning of the last verse is "not of those who have earned [Your] anger." Those who held that it is part of the Fatihah and of the surahs argued that it is written in the codex in the script of the Qur'an, and with what 'Abd al-Wahhab ibn Muhammad al-Kisa'i informed us: Abu Muhammad 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Ahmad al-Khallal informed us, Abu al-'Abbas Muhammad ibn Ya'qub al-Asamm informed us, al-Rabi' ibn Sulayman informed us, al-Shafi'i informed us, 'Abd al-Majid informed us, from Ibn Juraij, who said: my father informed me, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr [[Omitted from manuscript (A).]] concerning ﴿And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated and the great Qur'an﴾ (15:87): "It is Umm al-Qur'an." My father said: Sa'id ibn Jubayr recited it to me until he finished it, then he said: "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," the seventh verse. Sa'id said: I recited it to Ibn 'Abbas as I recited it to you, and he said: "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," the seventh verse. Ibn 'Abbas said: "He stored it up for you, and He did not bring it out for anyone before you." [[Related by al-Shafi'i in al-Musnad (1/79–80, ed. al-Sindi), and by the author in Sharh al-Sunnah (3/50). See also Talkhis al-Habir by Ibn Hajar (1/232).]]

Those who did not count it as part of the Fatihah argued with what Abu al-Hasan Muhammad ibn Muhammad al-Shirazi informed us: Zahir ibn Ahmad informed us, Abu 'Isa Ishaq al-Hashimi informed us, Abu Mus'ab informed us, from Malik, from Humayd al-Tawil, from Anas ibn Malik, may God be pleased with him, that he said: "I prayed behind Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may God be pleased with them, and all of them did not recite 'In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful' when they began the prayer." [[Related by Malik in al-Muwatta', chapter on what is done in recitation (1/81); and by the author in Sharh al-Sunnah (3/53–54); it is in Muslim's Sahih in the book of prayer, no. 399.]] Sa'id ibn Jubayr said, from Ibn 'Abbas: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) did not know the end of a surah until 'In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful' descended." [[Related by Abu Dawud in al-Marasil, p. 123; al-Hakim authenticated it according to their criteria (1/231). See also Talkhis al-Habir (1/233) and al-Durr al-Manthur (1/20).]]

And from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "We did not know the distinction between two surahs until 'In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful' descended." [[Related by al-Wahidi in al-Wasit (1/13) and in Asbab al-Nuzul, p. 54; al-Suyuti also attributed it to al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman. See al-Durr al-Manthur (1/20).]] Al-Sha'bi said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to write at the beginning of the matter in the script of Quraysh, 'In Your name, O God,' until there was revealed ﴿And he said: Embark therein; in the name of God is its course and its anchorage﴾ (11:41), so he wrote 'In the name of God,' until there was revealed ﴿Say: Call upon God or call upon the Most Gracious﴾ (17:110), so he wrote 'In the name of God, the Most Gracious,' until there was revealed ﴿Indeed, it is from Solomon, and indeed it is: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ (27:30), so he wrote the like of it."

His words: ﴿All praise is due to God﴾. Its wording is that of a report, as though it informs that the one deserving praise is God, Mighty and Majestic. It also contains a teaching for creatures, its estimated form being: "Say: All praise is due to God." *Al-hamd* may mean thanks for a favour, and it may mean praise of Him for the good qualities that are in Him. One says: "I praised so-and-so for what he bestowed upon me of favour," and "I praised him for his knowledge and his bravery." Thanks (*shukr*) is only for a favour, so *hamd* is more general than *shukr*, since one does not say "I thanked so-and-so for his knowledge." Thus every one who praises is thankful, but not every one who is thankful praises. It was said: *hamd* is with the tongue, in speech, and *shukr* is with the limbs, in action. God the Exalted said: ﴿And say: All praise is due to God, who has not taken a son﴾ (17:111), and He said: ﴿Work, O family of David, in thanks﴾ (34:13).

His words: ﴿to God﴾. The *lam* here indicates entitlement, as one says: "The house is for Zayd."

His words: ﴿Lord of the worlds, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾. *Rabb* may mean owner (*malik*), as one says to the owner of a house: "lord of the house." One says "lord of the thing" when he possesses it. It may also mean nurturing and improving: one says *rabba fulanun al-day'ah* (so-and-so nurtured the estate), *yarubbuha*, when he completed and improved it. So it is *rabb*, like *tabb* and *barr*. Thus God the Exalted is the owner of the worlds and their nurturer. The definite form *al-Rabb* is not said of a created being; rather one says *rabb kadha* (lord of such-and-such) in the construct form, because the definite article signifies generality, and a creature does not own everything.

"Al-'Alamin" is the plural of "'alam" (world), which has no singular form from its own root. Scholars differed about what al-'Alamin refers to. Ibn 'Abbas said: they are the jinn and humankind, because they are the ones addressed by the commands and prohibitions. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿That he may be a warner to the 'alamin﴾ (1 – al-Furqan). Qatadah, Mujahid and al-Hasan said: they are all created beings. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Pharaoh said, "And what is the Lord of the 'alamin?" He said, "Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them"﴾.

Its derivation is from "'ilm" (knowledge) and "'alamah" (sign), and they were so named because the effect of the Creator's craftsmanship is manifest in them. Abu 'Ubaydah said: they are four communities: the angels, humankind, the jinn and the devils. It is derived from "'ilm." Animals are not called 'alam, because they do not reason.

They differed about their number. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: "For Allah there are a thousand 'alam: six hundred in the sea and four hundred on land." Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: "For Allah there are eighty thousand 'alam: forty thousand in the sea and forty thousand on land." Wahb said: "For Allah there are eighteen thousand 'alam, of which this world is one. Civilization within ruin is only like a tent in a desert." Ka'b al-Ahbar said: "No one counts the number of the 'alamin except Allah." Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And none knows the hosts of your Lord except Him﴾ (31 – al-Muddaththir).

His saying: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾. 'Asim, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read ﴿Māliki﴾ (Master), and the others read ﴿Maliki﴾ (King). Some said: their meanings are the same, like "fārihīn" and "fārihīn" and "ḥadhirīn" and "ḥādhirīn," and their meaning is Lord; one says "rabb al-dar" (lord of the house) and "malikuha" (its owner). It was also said: "al-Malik" and "al-Mālik" both refer to the One who is able to bring things into existence from non-existence, and no one is able to do that except Allah. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "Malik" (Master) is more comprehensive and broader, because one says "malik al-'abd" (owner of the slave), "al-ṭayr" (of the birds) and "al-dawabb" (of the animals), but one does not say "malik" of these things. Also, one is not a master (mālik) of a thing unless one owns it, whereas one may be a king (malik) of a thing without owning it.

Others said: "Malik" is preferable, because every mālik is a malik, but not every malik is a mālik. Also, it is more consistent with the rest of the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿So exalted is Allah, the King, the Truth﴾ (114 – Ta-Ha), and ﴿the King, the Holy﴾ (23 – al-Hashr).

Mujahid said: "al-Din" is the reckoning. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿That is the upright religion﴾ (36 – al-Tawbah), meaning the upright reckoning. And "Maliki al-nas" (King of mankind) is in Surat al-Nas. Ibn 'Abbas, Muqatil and al-Suddi said: "Malik yawm al-din" means the judge of the Day of Reckoning. Qatadah said: "al-Din" is recompense, and it applies to recompense for good and evil alike; it is said: "As you judge, so you will be judged."

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: "King of a day on which none benefits except through religion [i.e., deeds]." Yaman ibn (Rabab) [in B: Rayyan] said: "al-Din" is subjugation. It is said: "danthu-hu fa-dāna," meaning "I subdued him, so he submitted in humility." It was also said: "al-Din" is obedience, that is, the Day of Obedience. The reason He specifically mentioned the Day of Judgment, though He is Master of all days, is that dominions will be extinct on that day, so there is no kingdom and no command except His. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The dominion that Day is true, for the Most Merciful﴾ (26 – al-Furqan), and He said: ﴿Whose is the dominion today? It is Allah's, the One, the Subduer﴾ (16 – Ghafir), and He said: ﴿And the command that Day belongs to Allah﴾ (19 – al-Infitar).

Abu 'Amr read ﴿al-Raḥīmi Maliki﴾ with the assimilation (idgham) of the "m" into the "m." Likewise he assimilates any two letters of the same type, or of the same or similar place of articulation, whether the letter is quiescent or vowelled, except when the first letter is doubled, nunated, has a short vowel, or the letter before it is a "ta" of address (taa' al-khitab) with a quiescent letter that is not a double letter; in such cases he does not assimilate them. Assimilation of a vowelled letter is in the "major assimilation" (al-idgham al-kabir). Hamzah agreed with him on assimilating a vowelled letter in His saying ﴿A party has plotted﴾ (81 – al-Nisa'), and ﴿By those who line up in rows, then those who drive away, then those who recite the reminder﴾ (1–3 – al-Saffat), and ﴿By the winnowing winds﴾ (1 – al-Dhariyat), where he assimilated the "ta" into the letter that follows it. Al-Kisa'i and Hamzah agreed on the assimilation of the minor kind, which is the assimilation of a quiescent letter into a vowelled one, except before the "ra" before "lam" and the "dal" before "jim." Likewise Hamzah does not assimilate the "dal" before "sin," "sad" and "zay" (according to the transmission of Khallad and Khalaf). There is no assimilation for the other readers except in a number of specified letters.

His saying ﴿Iyyaka na'budu﴾. "Iyya" is a pronoun particle that is specifically joined to a suffixed pronoun, and it is used before the verb, as in "Iyyaka a'nī" (It is You I mean) and "Iyyaka as'alu" (It is You I ask). It is not used after the verb except as a separate pronoun, as in "Ma 'anaytu illa iyyaka" (I meant none but You).

His saying ﴿na'budu﴾ means: we declare You one, and we obey You in humility. "Al-'ibadah" (worship) is obedience together with abasement and humility. The slave is called "'abd" because of his lowliness and submission, as in "ṭarīq mu'abbad," meaning a well-trodden path (lit. one made smooth).

﴿Wa iyyaka nasta'in﴾: we ask You for help in our worship and in all our affairs. If it is asked: why did He mention worship before seeking help, when seeking help comes before worship? This obliges those who hold that ability (istita'ah) precedes the act. But we, praise be to Allah, hold that success (tawfiq) and seeking help (al-isti'anah) occur together with the act, so there is no difference between the order of precedence and delay. It is said: seeking help is a kind of worship, so He mentioned the whole of worship first, and then mentioned what is among its details.

His saying: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾. "Ihdina" means "guide us," that is, direct us. 'Ali and Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: "Keep us firm," as one says to someone standing, "Stand until I return to you," meaning, remain in what you are upon. This supplication by believers, although they are already guided, carries the meaning of making firm and the meaning of seeking increase in guidance, because the divine favours and guidances from Allah the Exalted do not end, according to the doctrine of Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah).

"Al-Sirat" and "Siraṭ" with the "sin" is narrated by Uways from Ya'qub, and it is the original form. It was named "sirat" because it swallows (yasrutu) those who travel on it. It is also read with "zay," and Hamzah read it with the "zay" pronounced with a hint of "sin" (ishmam). All of them are valid dialects. The preferred reading, according to most readers, is with "sad," because it agrees with the Mushaf (the codex).

"Al-Sirat al-Mustaqim": Ibn 'Abbas and Jabir, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: it is Islam, and this is also the view of Muqatil. Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it is the Qur'an. [5/a] It was narrated from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) hadith: "The straight path is the Book of Allah." [Note: Al-Tabari recorded it in his Tafsir (1/171–172), and Shaykh Ahmad Shakir weakened it in his commentary on al-Tabari.] Sa'id ibn Jubayr, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it is the path to Paradise. Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah said: it is the path of the Sunnah and the Community (al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah). Bakr ibn 'Abd Allah al-Muzani said: it is the path of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. [Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Hasan said: the path of the Messenger of Allah, his family (aalihi) and his two companions.] [Note: omitted in B.] Its original linguistic meaning is the clear road.

His saying ﴿The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾: that is, those on whom You bestowed favour through guidance and success. 'Ikrimah said: You bestowed favour on them by steadfastness in faith and uprightness, and they are the Prophets, peace be upon them. It was also said: they are everyone whom Allah made firm in faith, among the Prophets and the believers, whom Allah mentioned in His saying: ﴿So those will be with those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour from among the prophets﴾ (69 – al-Nisa'), and so on. Ibn 'Abbas said: they are the people of Musa and 'Isa, peace be upon them both, before they changed their religion. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: they are the Prophet ﷺ and those with him. Abu al-'Aliyah said: they are the family of the Messenger ﷺ, Abu Bakr and 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, and his household. Shahr ibn Hawshab said: they are the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his household.

Hamzah read ﴿'alayhum, ladayhum, and ilayhum﴾ with the "h" vowel (ha') pronounced with a damma. Ya'qub pronounces with a damma each "ha'" preceded by a quiescent "ya'," in both the dual and the plural, except in His saying ﴿among their hands and their feet﴾ (12 – al-Mumtahanah). The others read them with a kasra. Those who pronounced the "ha'" with a damma returned it to its original form, because it is pronounced with a damma when standing alone. Those who pronounced it with a kasra did so because of the quiescent "ya'" and because the kasra is the sister of the "ya'." Ibn Kathir and Abu Ja'far pronounced every plural "mim" with a lengthened vowel (ishba') in continuous recitation when no quiescent letter follows it; if a quiescent letter follows it, they do not lengthen it. Nafi' has the choice. Warsh pronounces a damma before the hamzat al-qat' (the cut hamza); when it is followed by an alif of connection (alif al-wasl) and there is a kasra or a quiescent "ya'" before the "ha'," he pronounces the "ha'" and the "mim" with a damma. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i pronounce them both with a damma; Abu 'Amr pronounces them both with a kasra; likewise Ya'qub when the letter before it is kasra. The others read the "mim" with a damma and the "ha'" with a kasra in all cases, because of the "ya'" or because of the kasra before it, and the damma of the "mim" is on the original basis.

His saying: ﴿not of those who have evoked anger﴾: meaning the path of those upon whom You have been angry. Anger is the intention to take revenge on the disobedient. The anger of Allah the Exalted does not befall disobedient believers; it befalls only the disbelievers.

﴿Nor of those who are astray﴾: that is, and not of those who have gone astray from guidance. The root of "dalal" (going astray) is destruction and disappearance, as one says: "Dalla al-ma' fi al-laban" (the water was lost in the milk) when it perished and disappeared. Here "ghayr" means both "la" (not) and "ghayr" (other), and therefore it is permissible to coordinate with "wa" (and), as one says: "Fulan ghayr muhsin wa la mujmil" (So-and-so is not a doer of good nor of fair conduct). But when "ghayr" means "siwa" (other than), it is not permissible to join to it with "la," and one may not say in speech: "'Indi siwa 'Abd Allah wa la Zayd" (I have other than 'Abd Allah and not Zayd).

'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, read: "Sirat man an'amta 'alayhim ghayr al-maghdubi 'alayhim wa ghayr al-dallin" (the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, other than those upon whom anger is incurred, and other than those who go astray). It was said: "those upon whom anger is incurred" are the Jews, and "those who go astray" are the Christians, because Allah the Exalted judged the Jews to be under anger, saying: ﴿Whom Allah has cursed and upon whom He has become angry﴾ (60 – al-Ma'idah), and He judged the Christians to be astray, saying: ﴿And do not follow the desires of a people who had gone astray before﴾ (77 – al-Ma'idah). Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah said: "not of those who have evoked anger [upon them]" by innovation (bid'ah), and "nor of those who are astray" from the Sunnah.

It is the Sunnah for the reciter, after finishing the recitation of al-Fatihah, to say "Amin," with a separate pause apart from al-Fatihah. It is pronounced short, and according to the grammarians it may be read long or short. Its meaning is: "O Allah, hear and respond." Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: its meaning is "So let it be." Mujahid said: it is one of the names of Allah the Exalted. It was also said: it is the seal of supplication. It was also said: it is the seal of Allah upon His servants, by which He averts calamities from them, like the seal of a letter which prevents corruption and the disclosure of what is in it.

Al-Imam Abu 'Ali al-Husayn ibn Muhammad al-Qadi and Abu Hamid Ahmad ibn 'Abd Allah al-Salihi informed us, both saying: Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn Hasan al-Hiri informed us, Abu 'Ali Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Ma'qil al-Maydani narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated to us, 'Abd al-Razzaq narrated to us, Ma'mar informed us, from al-Zuhri, from Ibn al-Musayyab, from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "When the imam says '(not of those who have evoked anger) nor of those who are astray,' then say 'Amin,' for the angels say 'Amin,' and the imam says 'Amin.' Whoever's 'Amin' coincides with the 'Amin' of the angels, his previous sins will be forgiven." [Note: Al-Bukhari recorded it in al-Adhan, chapter on the imam's audible saying of amin (2/262); Ahmad narrated it (2/233) from Abu Hurayrah; al-Nasa'i in al-Iftitah, chapter on the imam's audible amin (2/144). The author also recorded it in Sharh al-Sunnah (3/61). In manuscript (A) there is an addition: "what was delayed" (ma ta'akhkhar).] Sahih.

Section on the virtue of al-Fatihah [in B: Fatihat al-Kitab].

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 1, verses 1–7 (part 3 of 3):

Abu al-Husayn Ahmad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad al-Kayyali told us: Abu Nasr Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Fadl al-Khuza'i told us: Abu Uthman Amr ibn Abd Allah al-Basri told us: Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab related to us: Khalid ibn Makhlad al-Qatawani related to us: Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn Abi Kathir, he being the brother of Isma'il ibn Ja'far, related to me, from al-Ala' ibn Abd al-Rahman, from his father, from Abu Hurayra, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ passed by Ubayy ibn Ka'b while he was standing and praying, so he called out to him, saying, 'Come here, O Ubayy!' Ubayy hastened in his prayer, then came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He said, 'What prevented you, O Ubayy, from answering me when I called you? Does Allah not say: ﴿O you who have believed, respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you to that which gives you life﴾ [al-Anfal 8:24]?' Ubayy said, 'Indeed, O Messenger of Allah, I will never fail to answer you again, even if I am praying.' He said, 'Would you like me to teach you a surah the like of which has not been revealed in the Torah, nor in the Gospel, nor in the Psalms, nor in the Qur'an?' Ubayy said, 'Yes, O Messenger of Allah.' He said, 'Do not leave the door of the mosque until you have learned it.' The Prophet ﷺ was walking, intending to leave the mosque, and when he reached the door to leave, Ubayy said to him, 'The surah, O Messenger of Allah!' So he stopped and said, 'Yes. How do you recite in your prayer?' Ubayy recited Umm al-Qur'an (the Mother of the Qur'an, i.e., al-Fatiha). The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, 'By Him in whose hand is my soul, there has not been revealed in the Torah, nor in the Gospel, nor in the Psalms, nor in the Qur'an, the like of it. It is indeed the seven oft-repeated (al-sab' al-mathani) which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has given me.'"
[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi in Fada'il al-Qur'an, chapter: What has come concerning the virtue of Fatihat al-Kitab, 8/178–180. Also Ahmad in al-Musnad: 2/412–413, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b. Ibn Khuzayma, 1/252, and Ibn Hibban in their Sahihs, and al-Hakim in summary, narrated from Abu Hurayra from Ubayy. Al-Hakim said: sahih according to the condition of Muslim (see al-Targhib wa al-Tarhib of al-Mundhiri, 2/367). The author also narrated it in Sharh al-Sunna: 4/446–447, and narrated something similar from Abu Sa'id ibn al-Mu'alla: al-Bukhari in al-Tafsir: 8/156.]] This is a hasan sahih (good, sound) hadith.

Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Abd al-Samad al-Turabi informed us: al-Hakim Abu al-Fadl Muhammad ibn al-Husayn al-Haddadi told us: Abu Yazid Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Khalid told us: Ishaq ibn Ibrahim al-Hanzali told us: Yahya ibn Adam related to us: Abu al-Ahwas related to us, from Ammar ibn Ruzayq, from Abd Allah ibn Isa, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "While the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was with Jibril (Gabriel) beside him, he heard a sound (naqid) from above him. Jibril, peace be upon him, raised his eyes to the sky and said, 'This is a gate that has been opened in the sky, which has never been opened before.' He said: A angel descended from it and came to the Prophet ﷺ and said, 'Rejoice in two lights which you have been given, which no prophet before you has been given: Fatihat al-Kitab and the final verses of Surat al-Baqara. You will not recite a single letter of them except that you will be given it.'"
[[Narrated by Muslim in Salat al-Musafirin, no. 806, chapter: The virtue of al-Fatiha and the final verses of Surat al-Baqara, 1/554. Also al-Nasa'i in Iftitah al-Salat, 2/138. The author also narrated it in Sharh al-Sunna: 4/466. And his saying "sam'a naqidan" means: a sound.]] Sahih (sound). [Narrated by Muslim from al-Hasan ibn Rabi' from Abu al-Ahwas.] [[Omitted from B.]]

Abu al-Hasan Muhammad ibn Muhammad al-Shirazi informed us: Zahir ibn Ahmad al-Sarakhsi related to us: Abu Ishaq Ibrahim ibn Abd al-Samad al-Hashimi informed us: Abu Mus'ab Ahmad ibn Abi Bakr al-Zuhri informed us, from Malik, from al-Ala' ibn Abd al-Rahman, that he heard Abu al-Sa'ib, client of Hisham ibn Zuhra, say: I heard Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, say: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever prays a prayer in which he does not recite Umm al-Qur'an, it is khidaj (deficient) — incomplete." He said: I said, "O Abu Hurayra, indeed I am sometimes behind the imam." He squeezed my forearm and said, "Recite it to yourself, O Persian, for I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: I have divided the prayer between Me and My servant into two halves; half of it is for Me and half of it is for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Recite. The servant says, "Al-hamdu lillahi rabbi al-alamin (All praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds)," and Allah says, "My servant has praised Me." The servant says, "Al-Rahman al-Rahim (The Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful)," and Allah says, "My servant has extolled Me." The servant says, "Maliki yawmi al-din (Master of the Day of Recompense)," and Allah says, "My servant has glorified Me." The servant says, "Iyyaka na'budu wa iyyaka nasta'in (You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help)," and Allah, Exalted is He, says, "This verse is between Me and My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks." The servant says, "Ihdina al-sirat al-mustaqim, sirat alladhina an'amta alayhim, ghayr al-maghdubi alayhim wa la al-dallin (Guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, not of those who have earned Your anger, nor of those who are astray)," and Allah says, "These are for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks.'"
[[Narrated by Muslim in al-Salat, chapter: The obligation of reciting al-Fatiha in every rak'a, no. 395, 1/296. The author also narrated it in Sharh al-Sunna: 3/47.]] Sahih (sound). [Narrated by Muslim from Qutayba from Malik.] [[Omitted from B.]]
